A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ECIF and retain matching methods, experiments, and appendices A-F. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison throughout; v2's reporting inconsistencies and truncated passages are document defects, not unavailable evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original CLIP experiments on data removal, accuracy and runtime, influential-data identification, misprediction tracing, and misalignment detection, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds attribution-method comparisons and results on CIFAR-100 and ANIMAL-10N.

M1.justification: Sections 4-5 and Algorithms 1-5 retain the same positive/negative influence components, Hessian-based updates, and influence scores. The new experiments and changed framing do not introduce a different method.

E1.justification: Appendices F.3-F.4 add CIFAR-100 utility/efficiency evaluation and ANIMAL-10N harmful-data removal. These extend coverage to additional object classes and naturally mislabeled, visually confusable animal populations, while retaining the original datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's retraining and random-removal comparisons, v2 evaluates IF-EKFAC, TRAK (printed as TARK), and TracIN on Flowers102 in Figure 3, and CLIPScore on Food101 in Figure 5. CLIPScore's earlier use as an evaluation function did not constitute this baseline comparison.

E3.justification: The added CLIPScore comparison evaluates harmful-removal ratios of 20%-50% in five-percentage-point steps, versus 20%-90% in ten-point steps in the retained random-removal comparison. Appendix F.2 specifies removing the least contributive 10% and retraining for the added attribution comparisons; the established CLIP/LoRA configuration remains.

E4.justification: Figures 4-5 extend removal-fraction sensitivity analyses to naturally noisy ANIMAL-10N and to ECIF versus CLIPScore. The existing multiple-sample removal analysis and qualitative tracing/misalignment examples are retained, sometimes relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: New Table 3 reports uncertainty for runtime, whereas v1's timing table reports single values. Conversely, v2 Appendix F.1 loses explicit three-seed repetition statements for valuable/harmful-data removal; Section 6.1 retains three runs for utility evaluation. No increase in run counts is established.

E6.justification: Table 3 and Figures 3-5 add substantial benchmark and comparator results. Table 1 preserves all accuracies but changes runtime entries: Food101 random-removal retraining/ECIF values change from 14.59/7.28 to 291.80/29.12. v2's conflicting seconds/minutes labels prevent interpreting these changes as comparable speed gains.

T1.justification: The influence derivations, relative-influence proposition, assumptions, Theorem D.7, and appendix proofs remain substantively unchanged. The linear-superposition assumption disappears from the main-text summary but remains explicit in Appendix D; notation and equation numbering changes do not establish new theory.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, first contribution, and conclusion redefine the claimed scope from multimodal large language models to contrastive learning. The abstract specifically attributes the empirical interpretability benefits to CLIP-style embedding models, materially narrowing that claim while retaining ECIF's central contribution and applications.

C2.justification: Appendix F.4 newly explains ECIF's advantage over CLIPScore through model-dependent attribution rather than data-quality scoring alone. F.3 also adds interpretations of CIFAR-100 accuracy and efficiency, although its numerical discussion conflicts with Table 3. No substantive new limitations analysis is added.

D1.justification: Appendix F.1 truncates the influential-data settings paragraph, losing its explicit three-seed repetitions and 0%-90% harmful-removal description. Most implementation information remains, including hardware, optimizer settings, LoRA rank, and the utility setup documented in Section 6.1.

R1.justification: v2 adds works by Grosse et al., Park et al., Pruthi et al., and Song et al. supporting the new comparisons and noise benchmark. The related-work narrative largely persists; duplicate or year-changed entries for already cited works do not represent additional research coverage.

P1.justification: The title, author list, abstract/introduction wording, and terminology are revised, an Impact Statement is added, and Appendix F gains subsections. Most exposition and section ordering remain intact, so the rewriting is limited despite the substantial visual reformatting.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout, substantially rearranging and resizing displays. v2 adds Figures 3-5 and the CIFAR-100 table, splits v1's Table 3 examples between Figures 2 and 8, and relocates retained qualitative examples and appendix plots.

improvement.justification: The more accurate CLIP-focused framing, competing attribution baselines, and added noisy-data evaluation improve scope alignment and empirical support. However, v2 introduces conflicting runtime units in Section 6 and Table 1, CIFAR-100 prose that disagrees with Table 3 in values and rankings, and losses of settings/run-count documentation in F.1. These problems affect central efficiency and validation claims, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
